narrative:
The model estimated an 80% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain; it means the application was assessed as carrying a very high risk under the school’s predictive criteria, so admission was denied.

The strongest factor was your third-year class rank: you are in the lowest decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile. That very low rank pushed the prediction strongly toward bar failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score of 24.5, well below the accepted-student average of about 37.2, which also pushed toward failure. The third factor was your first-year class rank, again the lowest decile versus an average near the sixth decile, adding further risk. Together, these academic indicators were the main reasons the model judged your bar-exam risk too high for admission.

To move forward, meet with an admissions adviser to discuss a realistic improvement plan. Focus first on preparing thoroughly and retaking the LSAT if possible, since a stronger score could materially change your profile. Also seek advice on coursework or other credentials that can demonstrate academic readiness, and consider programs with holistic review and strong bar-exam support. If you are admitted elsewhere, use academic support services early.
